prompt: Electric current is charge per unit time, I = Δ Q over Δ t, and one ampere is one coulomb per {{1}}.
explanation: One second. 1 A = 1 C/s, straight from the definition. It is why the CD-player question can go from a current and a time to a charge in one multiplication.

prompt: Ohm's law is V = IR, and one ohm is one volt per amp.
explanation: True on both. Cover the quantity you want and the formula rearranges itself: cover V and you see IR, cover I and you see V over R. The unit follows from the same relation, since R = V/I gives volts per amp.

why.true: Correct on both the formula and the unit.
why.false: Wrong. V = IR is the definition, and rearranging it to R = V/I gives the unit directly.

prompt: Resistance from resistivity is R = ρ L over A, so a wire that is long and thin has a {{1}} resistance than one that is short and fat.
explanation: Higher. L is on top so length raises it, and A is underneath so width lowers it. The water-hose picture makes it stick: a long narrow hose fights the flow, a short wide one hardly does.

prompt: Resistors in series simply add, and the same current flows through every one of them.
explanation: True on both, and the two facts are linked: there is only one path, so the current has nowhere else to go, and each resistor adds its own opposition to that single path. Test 1 question 12 depends on it, where naming R3 invites you to divide 48 by 3 when the answer is the whole loop's current.

why.true: Correct. One path, one current, and the resistances add.
why.false: Wrong. Series is the case where they DO simply add; it is parallel that combines reciprocally.

prompt: Resistors in parallel combine reciprocally, and the answer is always {{1}} than the smallest resistor in the group.
explanation: Less. Adding another path can only make it easier for current to flow, never harder. It is a free check on every parallel answer: if your total is not below the smallest, you forgot to flip the reciprocal back at the end.

prompt: For exactly two resistors in parallel, R equivalent = R1 R2 over R1 + R2, product over sum.
explanation: True, and it is worth memorising because two-resistor parallel groups appear constantly. It is only a shortcut for TWO: with three or more you must go back to the reciprocal sum. Checking it on 100 and 200 ohms gives 20000 over 300 = 66.7 ohms, duly below the smaller.

why.true: Correct, and product over sum is the phrase to remember.
why.false: Wrong. It follows algebraically from the reciprocal rule when there are exactly two.

prompt: In the voltage divider V1 = R1 over R total, times V, the resistor on top is the {{1}} one.
explanation: The WANTED one, the resistor whose voltage you are after. That is the opposite of the current divider, where the OTHER resistor goes on top. Getting them the wrong way round is the single commonest circuit error, and both wrong answers usually appear as options.

prompt: In the current divider for two resistors, the resistor that appears on top of the fraction is the OTHER one, not the one whose current you want.
explanation: True, and it is the mirror image of the voltage divider. I1 = R2 over R1 + R2, times I total. The physical sense is that current prefers the easier path, so the SMALLER resistor takes the LARGER share, which only works out if the other resistance sits on top.

why.true: Correct. Other resistor on top, which is why the smaller resistor carries more current.
why.false: Wrong. Putting the wanted resistor on top is the VOLTAGE divider rule, and it would wrongly give the bigger resistor the bigger current.

prompt: Kirchhoff's current law says the currents into a junction equal the currents out of it, which is conservation of {{1}}.
explanation: Charge. Nothing accumulates at a junction, so whatever arrives must leave. The partner law, the voltage law around a loop, is conservation of ENERGY. KCL is charge, KVL is energy, and keeping the pair straight is what makes the two-loop problems tractable.

prompt: Kirchhoff's voltage law says the sum of the potential differences around any closed loop is zero, and it expresses conservation of energy.
explanation: True. Go all the way round a loop and you arrive back where you started, so the total change in potential must be nothing, exactly as walking a closed path on a hillside returns you to your starting height. The rises across sources balance the drops across resistors.

why.true: Correct, and the closed-path argument is why it must be exactly zero.
why.false: Wrong. Returning to the same point means returning to the same potential, so the sum cannot be anything but zero.

prompt: The ampere is the unit of current, and it equals one coulomb per second.
explanation: True, and it is simply the definition I = Δ Q over Δ t read as units. The slides note that a 1 A current is fairly strong, and that phones and music players run on small fractions of an amp.

why.true: Correct. One coulomb of charge passing each second.
why.false: Wrong. That IS the definition of the ampere.

prompt: In circuit language, what is a BRANCH?

options.text: A single element such as a resistor or a source
A point where two or more conductors meet

explanation: A branch is one element. A junction, or node, is a meeting point, and a loop is a closed path. The three words are the vocabulary Kirchhoff's laws are written in: the current law works at junctions and the voltage law around loops.

why.a: Correct. A branch is one element, such as a single resistor or a single source.
why.b: Wrong. That is a junction or node.
why.d: Wrong. That is a short circuit.
why.e: Wrong. A circuit contains many branches.

prompt: A material is called {{1}} when it obeys Ohm's law, with its resistance constant at a fixed temperature.
explanation: Ohmic. Metal wires and ordinary resistors are ohmic; semiconductors are the important exception the slides name, because their resistance falls as they warm. The temperature qualification matters: even a metal stops being ohmic if you let it heat up.

prompt: A semiconductor sits between a conductor and an insulator, and unlike a metal its resistance {{1}} as it heats.
explanation: Falls. Heating a metal makes its atoms jiggle and collide with electrons, raising resistance; heating a semiconductor frees more charge carriers, which wins. That backwards behaviour is why semiconductors are the standing exception to Ohm's law in this course.

prompt: A short circuit has zero resistance, so it carries all the current and bypasses everything in parallel with it.
explanation: True. A parallel combination can never exceed its smallest member, so a zero-resistance branch pulls the whole section to zero and everything beside it is bypassed. With almost no resistance left the current climbs until something fails, which is why a short circuit is a hazard rather than a curiosity.

why.true: Correct, and it follows directly from the parallel rule.
why.false: Wrong. Current takes the easiest path, and zero resistance is as easy as it gets.
